title: The Power of Small Habits
speaker: James Carter
description: 微小习惯如何日积月累改变你的人生
transcript:
Good evening, everyone. I want to start with a simple question. Have you ever decided to change your life completely starting tomorrow? Maybe you decided to wake up at five in the morning, run for an hour, eat nothing but vegetables, and read a hundred pages of a book. And how long did that last? For most of us, about three days.

The problem is not that we lack willpower. The problem is that we are trying to change too much, too fast. Tonight, I want to talk about a different approach to change, one that is so small it almost seems too simple to work. I call it the power of small habits.

Let me give you an example. A few years ago, I wanted to get fit. I bought a gym membership, planned to go every day for an hour. I went three times in the first week, twice in the second, and by the third week, I had completely stopped. The gym membership became a monthly donation to a business I never visited.

Then I tried something different. I decided to do just one push-up every morning. One. Not ten, not twenty. Just one. And here is the interesting part. Most days, once I was on the floor doing that one push-up, I ended up doing five or ten. But even on the days I only did one, I had still exercised. The habit was established.

Within three months, I was doing thirty push-ups every morning without thinking about it. The one push-up had grown into something substantial, but it started so small that I never resisted it.

This is the first principle of small habits: make it so easy that you cannot say no. When a habit is tiny, it does not require motivation. It does not require willpower. It requires almost no effort. And because it requires no effort, you do it every day. And doing something every day, even something small, is what creates change.

The second principle is about compound interest. We understand compound interest with money. A small amount, invested regularly over time, grows exponentially. The same is true of habits. If you improve by just one percent every day for a year, you will be thirty-seven times better by the end of that year. Not one percent better. Thirty-seven times better. That is the mathematics of compound improvement.

But here is the difficult part. In the beginning, the results are invisible. If you save a dollar a day, after a week you have seven dollars. That does not feel like progress. If you read one page a day, after a week you have read seven pages. That does not feel like a book. And this is where most people quit. They quit because they cannot see the results yet.

I want you to think about how ice melts. If you have a block of ice at twenty-five degrees Fahrenheit, it is still solid ice. You raise the temperature to thirty degrees. Still solid. Thirty-two degrees. Still solid. But at thirty-three degrees, suddenly it begins to melt. The one-degree change from thirty-two to thirty-three seems small, but it is the tipping point. All the warming from twenty-five to thirty-two was stored, waiting. It was not wasted. It was building toward the moment of change.

Habits work the same way. The early days, the early weeks, feel like nothing is happening. But you are storing energy. You are raising the temperature. And then, one day, the ice melts. The change becomes visible.

The third principle is about identity. Most people focus on what they want to achieve. I want to run a marathon. I want to lose twenty pounds. I want to write a book. But the most effective way to change your behavior is to change who you believe you are. Instead of saying I want to run a marathon, say I am a runner. Instead of I want to write a book, say I am a writer.

When you change your identity, your habits follow naturally. A runner does not have to force themselves to run. A writer does not have to force themselves to write. The behavior becomes an expression of who they are, not a task they are trying to complete.

And here is the beautiful thing. Every time you do a small habit, you are casting a vote for that identity. One push-up is a vote for being an athlete. One page read is a vote for being a reader. One sentence written is a vote for being a writer. You do not need to cast every vote. You just need to cast most of them.

So tonight, I want to leave you with one challenge. Pick one thing you want to change. Not ten things. One thing. And make it ridiculously small. If you want to exercise, do one push-up. If you want to read, read one page. If you want to meditate, sit quietly for one minute. Do it tomorrow morning. And the morning after that. Do not worry about the results. The results will come, in time, the way ice melts when the temperature is right.

Thank you.

title: Why Sleep Matters More Than You Think
speaker: Dr. Sarah Mitchell
description: 睡眠对身体和大脑的深远影响
transcript:
Good afternoon. Let me ask you a question. How many of you got eight hours of sleep last night? Let me guess. Not many. And I understand. We live in a world that celebrates busy. We wear our exhaustion like a badge of honor. We say things like, I will sleep when I am dead. Well, tonight, I want to tell you that the shorter your sleep, the sooner that day may come.

I am a neuroscientist, and I have spent the last fifteen years studying sleep. And what I have discovered is that sleep is not a luxury. It is not an indulgence. It is the most important thing you can do for your brain and your body. Every major organ, every system in your body, is enhanced by sleep and impaired by a lack of it.

Let us start with the brain. When you are awake, your brain is constantly producing metabolic waste. These are toxic byproducts of neural activity. During the day, this waste accumulates. If it is not cleared away, it damages the brain. Now, your brain has a cleaning system called the glymphatic system. And here is the remarkable thing. This system is active almost exclusively during deep sleep.

Think of your brain like a city. During the day, the city is busy. Traffic is flowing, factories are running, waste is being produced. At night, when the city quietens down, the sanitation workers come out. They clear the streets, remove the waste, and prepare the city for the next day. If the sanitation workers do not come, the waste accumulates. The streets become filthy. The city cannot function properly.

That is what happens to your brain when you do not sleep. The waste accumulates. And one of the proteins that accumulates is called amyloid-beta. Amyloid-beta is the same protein that builds up in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. In fact, studies have shown that people who chronically sleep less than six hours a night have a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

Now let us talk about learning and memory. You probably know that you need sleep after learning to consolidate new information. But what you may not know is that you also need sleep before learning, to prepare your brain to absorb new information like a dry sponge. We did a study where we had two groups of people. One group slept a full eight hours. The other group was kept awake all night. The next day, we showed them new information to learn. The sleep-deprived group had a forty percent deficit in their ability to form new memories. Forty percent. That is the difference between an A and a failing grade.

And it gets worse. Sleep deprivation does not just affect your brain. It affects your entire body. After just one night of four hours of sleep, the number of natural killer cells in your immune system drops by seventy percent. Natural killer cells are your body's defense against infections and tumors. After one week of sleeping five hours instead of eight, testosterone levels in men drop to levels equivalent to aging ten years. Insulin sensitivity, which is crucial for regulating blood sugar, decreases significantly. You become, in a very real sense, metabolically older.

And then there is the cardiovascular system. We studied the effect of daylight saving time on heart attacks. In the spring, when we lose an hour of sleep, heart attacks spike by twenty-four percent the following day. In the autumn, when we gain an hour, heart attacks drop by twenty-one percent. One hour of sleep, in one direction or another, produces a measurable change in cardiovascular health. That is how sensitive the human body is to sleep.

So what is the solution? First, prioritize sleep. Treat it with the same respect you give to your work or your family. Second, consistency is key. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, even on weekends, is one of the most effective things you can do. Third, create a cool, dark environment. Your bedroom should be cool, around eighteen degrees Celsius. Your brain needs to drop its core temperature to initiate sleep. Fourth, avoid screens before bed. The blue light suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals your brain that it is time to sleep. And fifth, avoid caffeine late in the day. Caffeine has a half-life of five to seven hours. That cup of coffee at four in the afternoon is still in your system at ten or eleven at night.

Sleep is not the enemy of productivity. It is the foundation of it. The most productive people, the most creative people, the healthiest people, are almost always the best sleepers. So tonight, I want you to do one thing. Go to bed an hour earlier. Your brain, your body, and your future self will thank you.

Thank you.

title: The Hidden World of Coral Reefs
speaker: Dr. David Chen
description: 珊瑚礁的生态价值与面临的危机
transcript:
Hello, everyone. I want to take you on a journey to a place that most of you have never seen, but which is more important to your survival than you might imagine. I am talking about coral reefs.

Now, when I say coral reef, what do you picture? Probably a beautiful underwater scene. Colorful fish, clear blue water, maybe a sea turtle gliding by. And that image is correct. But it is only a tiny fraction of the story. Coral reefs are not just beautiful. They are one of the most complex, most ancient, and most valuable ecosystems on our planet.

Let me give you some perspective. Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor. Less than one percent. And yet, they are home to twenty-five percent of all marine species. One quarter of all life in the ocean depends on reefs for survival. If reefs disappear, those species disappear. It is that simple.

But the importance of reefs goes far beyond biodiversity. Let us talk about economics. Coral reefs provide economic value to humans worth approximately three hundred and seventy-five billion dollars per year. They support fishing industries that feed hundreds of millions of people. They protect coastlines from storms and erosion, reducing wave energy by up to ninety-seven percent. Without reefs, coastal cities from Miami to Mumbai would face far greater damage from hurricanes and typhoons.

And then there is medicine. You have probably heard that many medicines come from plants on land. But did you know that some of the most promising medical breakthroughs are coming from coral reefs? A compound derived from a sponge found on Caribbean reefs is already used in a drug that treats certain types of cancer. Another compound, from a soft coral, is being developed as an anti-inflammatory agent. Reefs are a living pharmacy, and we have barely begun to explore their potential.

So what exactly is a coral reef? It is a living structure built by tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp is about the size of a pinhead. It secretes a calcium carbonate skeleton, and over thousands of years, these skeletons accumulate, building the massive structures we call reefs. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia, for example, is so large that it can be seen from space. It is the largest living structure on Earth.

But here is the part that most people do not understand. The coral polyp itself is colorless. The brilliant colors of a reef come from tiny algae called zooxanthellae that live inside the coral's tissue. These algae photosynthesize, converting sunlight into food, and they share up to ninety percent of that food with the coral. In return, the coral provides the algae with a safe home and the nutrients they need. It is one of the most remarkable partnerships in nature.

And this partnership is fragile. When the ocean gets too warm, the coral becomes stressed. And when coral is stressed, it expels the algae. Without the algae, the coral loses its color. It turns white. This is what we call coral bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. It has lost its primary source of food. If the temperature returns to normal quickly, the coral can recover. If it does not, the coral dies.

And this is happening on a massive scale. In 2016 and 2017, the Great Barrier Reef experienced back-to-back bleaching events that affected nearly half of the reef. In the Caribbean, coral cover has declined by eighty percent over the past four decades. Globally, we have lost about half of the world's coral reefs in the past thirty years. Let me repeat that. We have lost half of the world's coral reefs in thirty years.

The primary cause is climate change. When ocean temperatures rise even one or two degrees above normal, corals bleach. And as global temperatures continue to rise, these events are becoming more frequent and more severe. What used to happen once a decade now happens every few years. The coral does not have time to recover.

But there is hope. Scientists around the world are working on solutions. Some are breeding heat-resistant coral in laboratories and transplanting it onto degraded reefs. Others are developing techniques to cool small areas of reef during heat waves. Marine protected areas, where fishing and other human activities are restricted, give reefs the best chance to recover and adapt.

But ultimately, the fate of coral reefs depends on what we do about climate change. If we can limit global warming to one and a half degrees above pre-industrial levels, as the Paris Agreement calls for, we may save a significant portion of the world's reefs. If we fail, we could lose virtually all of them by the end of this century.

So the next time you hear about coral reefs, I want you to remember this. They are not just pretty underwater scenery. They are the foundation of marine life, the protector of our coasts, a source of medicine, and a living structure that has existed for millions of years. They are worth fighting for. And the fight is not over yet.

Thank you.

title: The Bias We Don't See: How Mental Shortcuts Shape Our Decisions
speaker: Prof. Thomas Reid
description: 认知偏差如何不知不觉影响我们的判断与选择
transcript:
Right, so before we start, I want you to picture something. You walk into a car dealership, yeah? You've done your research, you know roughly what the car's worth, and you're feeling pretty confident. Then the salesman names a price, and suddenly every number after that feels like a bargain compared with the first one. Well, that right there is the first thing I want to talk about today, 'cause it sets up everything else.

I'm Thomas Reid, and I study the shortcuts our brains take when we're making decisions. You know, we like to think of ourselves as rational creatures, don't we? We weigh the evidence, we compare the options, we pick the sensible one. But here's the awkward truth: most of the time we're not doing that at all. We're running on autopilot, and we're sorta proud of it, actually, because it's fast and it feels good.

Let me give you a proper example. There was this study — I'm gonna simplify it a bit — where researchers asked people to estimate how many African countries were in the United Nations. But first they spun a wheel, a literal wheel of fortune, that landed on either ten or sixty. Totally random, had nothing to do with the question. Well, the people who saw sixty gave much higher estimates than the people who saw ten. I mean, they knew the wheel was random. Everyone did. And still, that meaningless number stuck in their heads like glue. That's what we call anchoring, and, um, it's sneaky precisely because you don't feel it happening.

Now, anchoring's just the beginning. Once you've got an anchor, your brain goes looking for evidence that supports it. You know how it is — you decide someone's a bit of a jerk in the first five minutes, and then suddenly everything they do confirms it. They're late? Obviously they're a jerk. They hold the door for someone? Well, they're probably just showing off, sort of trying to look good in front of others. That's confirmation bias, and it's basically a filter you didn't know you'd switched on.

And here's the thing about confirmation bias: it doesn't just affect your opinion of people. It affects what you read, who you follow, which news you trust. You've probably noticed, like, your social media feed kind of agrees with you, right? That's not an accident, and it's not the algorithm being clever — well, not entirely. It's you clicking on the stuff that feels right and scrolling past the stuff that doesn't. We're building our own little echo chambers, one click at a time. Simple as that.

Okay, so let's talk about the third shortcut, and this one's my favourite, I gotta admit. It's called the availability heuristic. Basically, we judge how likely something is by how easily we can picture it. So after a plane crash on the news, everybody's terrified of flying, even though, statistically, driving to the airport is way more dangerous. I mean, you can't picture a thousand uneventful car journeys, can you? But one dramatic crash, that sticks. And the media, well, they're not exactly going to report on the plane that landed safely, are they? Right, so the vivid story wins every time over the dull statistics.

Now here's where it gets interesting, and this is the bit that always surprises my students. You might think, right, now I know about these biases, I'll be fine. I'll just avoid them. But that's not how it works. Knowing about a bias doesn't switch it off. There was a study where they told people all about confirmation bias, in detail, and then gave them a task — and they fell for it just as badly as everyone else. I'm not making this up. It's almost like the knowledge becomes another tool you use to feel smart while you're making the exact same mistake. Look, I've been guilty of it myself. I once wrote a whole article arguing that a certain policy was doomed, and I only cited sources that agreed with me. I felt so clever. And then a colleague pointed out, very politely, that I'd ignored half the evidence. I dunno, maybe I was just embarrassed, but it took me a while to accept it.

So where does that leave us? Am I telling you we're all doomed to be irrational? Not quite. The trick isn't to eliminate these shortcuts — you can't, they're built in, and honestly you wouldn't want to, because without them you'd never get out of bed in the morning. The trick is to notice them. When you catch yourself feeling really, really certain about something, that's exactly the moment to pause. Ask yourself: what would it take to change my mind? If the answer's nothing, well, you're probably in the grip of a bias. And that, my friends, is a genuinely useful skill. It's not glamorous, it's not gonna win you arguments at parties, but it's the best defence we've got. Thank you.

title: What Ancient Rome Can Teach Us About Modern Concrete
speaker: Dr. Emily Hartley
description: 古罗马混凝土的耐久之谜及其对现代工程的启示
transcript:
G'day everyone, and thanks for coming along. Now, I want you to imagine you're standing in the middle of Rome, right, surrounded by buildings that have been there for two thousand years. The Pantheon's still got the largest unreinforced concrete dome on the planet, and it's been standing since, well, since before anyone here was even a twinkle in their parents' eyes. So here's my question for you today: how on earth did they do it?

I'm Emily Hartley, and I look at ancient materials — well, mostly I look at why the Romans were better at making concrete than we are. And I know that sounds a bit odd, because, you know, we've got all this modern technology, we've got steel and computers and, like, super-strong cement. You'd think we'd have nailed it. But honestly, our concrete starts falling apart after fifty or a hundred years. The Romans? Some of their stuff is still basically brand new after two millennia. I'm not exaggerating — go and have a look at the harbour at Pozzuoli. The piers are still there, underwater, and they're fine. Not bad for a very old trick.

Right, so what's the difference? Well, for ages, people assumed the Romans just had some secret ingredient we'd lost track of. Maybe it was a special volcanic ash from a particular mountain, or, um, I dunno, some magic additive. And there was a bit of truth to that — they did use volcanic ash, this stuff called pozzolana, which reacts with lime and water to form a really durable cement. But here's the thing: we know about pozzolana. We can buy the stuff. So that alone doesn't explain why theirs outlasts ours by such a huge margin, like forty times longer.

The real breakthrough, and this is what got me properly excited, came from looking really closely at the material under a microscope. You see, Roman concrete has these little white bits in it, these chalky lumps of lime. And for years, scientists looked at those and thought, right, that's a defect. That's sloppy mixing, kinda carelessness. I mean, you're not supposed to have chunks of unreacted lime in your concrete, are you? It's gotta be a mistake. Well, it turns out those lumps are the whole point.

Here's how it works, and I'm gonna keep this simple. When water gets into a crack — and water always gets into cracks, that's what water does — it dissolves those lime lumps. Then the dissolved lime reacts with the volcanic ash and forms new crystals that fill the crack back up. So the concrete, sort of, heals itself. It's like it's got its own immune system. How cool is that? And the Romans did this on purpose, probably. They used a technique we now call hot mixing, where they added the lime really hot, almost boiling, which created those brittle little clasts. So what looked like a flaw was actually a feature. Makes you think, doesn't it?

Now, there's an important contrast I want you to hold in your head, because this is where the modern stuff falls down. Our concrete is reinforced with steel bars, right, rebar. It makes it incredibly strong, initially. But steel rusts. And when it rusts, it expands, and when it expands, it cracks the concrete from the inside. So our buildings are, basically, fighting a losing battle against their own skeleton. The Romans didn't use steel at all. Their concrete was kinda weaker in the short term, but it got stronger over time, and it could last for centuries without falling apart. So, you know, there's a real lesson in there about trading short-term strength for long-term survival.

And here's the twist I didn't expect when I started this research. We've actually started making self-healing concrete in the lab now, inspired by the Romans. But it's tricky, 'cause modern building rules are written for concrete that behaves a certain predictable way, and this new stuff behaves differently. So the barrier isn't really scientific any more. It's bureaucratic. We've known, or at least suspected, the secret for a decade, and we're still arguing about paperwork. Wanna guess how long that's taken?

So what do I want you to take away? Not that we should all go back to building like the Romans — I'm not saying that, and honestly their buildings weren't exactly comfy. I'm saying that sometimes the answer to a modern problem is sitting in the past, and we walk past it because we've decided we're more clever than our ancestors. We're not, always. Look, next time you walk past an old building, don't just see a relic. See a bit of engineering that's still teaching us. Right, thank you very much.

title: The Business of Free: Why "No Charge" Often Costs You More
speaker: Rachel Simmons
description: 免费商业模式背后的隐性代价与数据经济
transcript:
Hey everyone, so let me start with a question. How many free apps are on your phone right now? Go on, actually count them in your head. I'll wait. Right, probably more than you think. And here's the thing: none of those companies are charities. Nobody's paying your electricity bill out of the goodness of their heart. So the real question isn't whether something's free. It's what you're giving up in exchange. That's what I wanna talk about today, and I promise you'll look at that phone of yours a little differently by the time I've finished.

I'm Rachel Simmons, and I study digital business models — basically, how companies make money when they don't charge you a cent. And, you know, the word 'free' is doing an enormous amount of work in our economy. It's like this magic label that makes us stop thinking. You see 'free download' and your brain goes, well, there's no downside, right? Simple as that. But that's exactly the reaction these companies are counting on.

Let me give you an example I use with my students. There's this whole genre of mobile games that are, technically, free. You download them, you play them, you don't pay anything. But then you hit a level you can't beat, and the game says, hey, you wanna an extra life? Just watch this thirty-second ad. Or, you know, you can pay two dollars to skip it. Now, think about what's actually happening there. The company isn't really selling you a game. It's selling your attention to advertisers. And the 'free' players? They're the product, not the customer. I mean, that sounds harsh, but it's basically true.

Now, there's another layer to this, and this is where it gets a bit more serious. A lot of these services aren't collecting your money — they're collecting you. I'm talking about your data. Where you go, what you buy, who your friends are, what time you go to bed. And, look, individually none of that sounds threatening. Who cares if an app knows I like coffee? But when you put millions of those little pieces together, you get something incredibly valuable. Companies will pay serious money for a detailed picture of your habits. So the price of 'free' isn't dollars, it's information about your life. And that, honestly, is worth more to them than a few dollars ever would be.

Here's another thing worth mentioning — the free trial. You've all seen it, right? 'Try it free for thirty days.' And the whole design is built around you forgetting to cancel. I'm not gonna say it's a scam, but, um, let's just say the odds are not exactly in your favour. They're betting that you'll get used to the product, and then, boom, you're paying. And cancelling? That's deliberately made awkward. I once spent, well, I dunno, twenty minutes trying to cancel a subscription I'd signed up for in, like, two clicks. That's not an accident. That's a business model. Crazy, right?

So where's the surprise, you ask? Well, here's the bit that really gets me. We complain about the cost, but we rarely complain about the thing that actually costs us most — our time. Think about it. You're scrolling through a free feed, and an hour disappears. That hour is the most valuable thing you own, and you traded it for, what, a few jokes and some cat videos? The money you didn't spend is trivial compared with the time you did. And the companies know it. Their entire goal is to keep you on the platform as long as possible. Every minute you spend is another minute of data, another ad, another chance to sell you something.

Look, I'm not saying never use free stuff. That'd be ridiculous — some of it's genuinely brilliant, and I use plenty of it myself. All I'm asking is that you go in with your eyes open. Ask yourself: if I'm not paying, what am I actually paying with? Is it my data? My attention? My time? And read the terms — I know, I know, nobody reads the terms — but just skim the important bits. 'Cause a little scepticism goes a long way. Your attention's not worthless. It's the most valuable currency you've got. Spend it like you mean it. Thank you.

title: Bringing Wild Nature Back to Our Cities
speaker: James Whitfield
description: 城市再野化：让自然重新进入城市的设计与实践
transcript:
Right, so before we begin, I want you to try something. Picture a typical city street in your head — the cars, the pavements, the shop fronts, maybe a pigeon pecking at a dropped chip. Now, where's the wild stuff? I mean the frogs, the tall grass, the beetles hiding under a stone. You probably can't, can you? And that, my friends, is the whole reason I wanna talk to you today.

I'm James Whitfield, and I spend my days thinking about how we can let nature back into the places we've built. We usually call it rewilding. Now, I know what you're thinking — surely that just means planting a few trees and, like, making it look nice? Well, no, not really. It's a bit subtler than that, and, um, it's also a lot more interesting than it sounds.

Here's the basic idea. A conventional park is designed. Someone decides where every shrub goes, which grass to mow, which path to lay. It's nice, don't get me wrong, but it's kinda like a garden on a grand scale. Rewilding flips that. It's sort of the opposite of gardening — you step back, you remove the fences and the concrete, and then you let natural processes take over. You let the river flood where it wants to. You let the plants compete and the beetles arrive on their own. The job of us humans is mostly to get out of the way. Sounds simple, right? Actually, it's harder than it sounds, and I'm gonna come back to why in a minute.

Let me give you an example that still blows my mind. There was an old rail yard in a European city — a big concrete slab that had been abandoned for decades. Nobody looked after it. Then, gradually, weeds started pushing through the cracks, then shrubs, then small trees. Birds came. And here's the number I want you to hold onto: within about twenty years, more than a hundred and fifty species of bird had been recorded there. A hundred and fifty! On a piece of ground that everyone had written off as useless. And the remarkable thing isn't just the number. It's that nobody planted any of it. We didn't do the hard work. We just stopped interfering, and the place healed itself. Not bad, eh?

So that's the first lesson: nature is stubborn, and it's waiting quietly under our pavements. But rewilding isn't only about having more birds around, though that's a lovely bonus. There are practical reasons too. A city with more trees and wild ground is a cooler city — I don't mean cooler in the trendy sense. I mean actual degrees. Concrete bakes in summer, but plants shade the ground and release water, so the whole neighbourhood drops in temperature. And when heavy rain comes, wild soil soaks it up instead of sending it straight outta the drains into the river. So you get fewer floods as well. Simple as that.

And there's a human side to this as well, which I care about a lot. When people get a bit of genuine green space — not a manicured lawn, but somewhere a bit messy and alive — they report feeling calmer, less stressed. You know how it feels when you hear birds in the morning rather than traffic? That's not nothing. A city that's good for wildlife turns out to be good for us too. Funny how that works.

Now here's the twist, and this is the bit that genuinely surprises people. You'd think the hard part would be the science — working out which plants to encourage, how to move animals back. But it's not. The science is mostly sorted. The real obstacle is us. You see, we've got this idea in our heads that nature should look tidy. A wild patch looks untidy. It looks, uh, unfinished. And the moment it looks a bit scruffy, someone complains. I've seen it a hundred times — a council leaves a corner of a park to grow wild, and, well, I dunno, within a week there are letters saying it looks like a mess, that nobody's maintaining it. But that mess is exactly the point. We've confused being cared for with being neat, and those two things aren't the same at all.

So where does that leave us? Look, I'm not saying we should turn every city centre into a jungle — some of us still need somewhere to park a bus. What I'm saying is that we can leave a little more room for the wild. Let the verge grow. Put a pond in, even a tiny one. Accept that a hedge doesn't need trimming every fortnight — you've gotta let it be a bit messy sometimes. 'Cause the truth is, we don't need to do more. We mostly need to do less, and then be patient. Nature's been at this a lot longer than we have. It knows what it's doing. Give it half a chance and it'll surprise you. Thank you very much.

options: To argue that city planners ought to spend far more money on decorative public gardens.
To draw attention to how thoroughly nature has vanished from the places people know best.
To suggest that pigeons are the only wild creatures still able to survive in built-up areas.

You probably can't, can you?' 讲话人用'街上有蛙、草、甲虫吗？你想不出来'开场，是为了让我们意识到自然已从最熟悉的日常场景里消失。答案 B 的 'how thoroughly nature has vanished from the places people know best' 是对这层的同义概括——'vanished' 对应 'you can't [picture them]'，'places people know best' 对应 'a typical city street'，没有照搬原词。干扰项 A 说'应该花钱建装饰性花园'，恰恰与后文'公园像大号花园、但再野化不是这样'相反；C 把随口提到的鸽子当成'唯一能存活的野生动物'，是抓住原文细节的断章取义；D 说'只是逗乐热身'，低估了开场设问的论证功能，迷惑性在于它确实是引入话题，但答非所问。

questions.question: According to the speaker, what does rewilding actually involve in practice, as opposed to designing a conventional garden?
options: Stepping back so natural processes can re-establish themselves with little human direction.
Carefully selecting native plants and arranging them within neatly structured public spaces.
Bringing in specialists to manage every single stage of a habitat's recovery in detail.
Turning whole city centres into dense woodland while preserving the existing road network.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'It's sort of the opposite of gardening — you step back, you remove the fences and the concrete, and then you let natural processes take over.' 后面又说 'We didn't do the hard work. We just stopped interfering.' 推理链：再野化的核心不是'做更多'，而是'人类退后、让自然自己恢复'。答案 A 的 'stepping back so natural processes can re-establish themselves with little human direction' 精准同义替换（step back → stepping back，let natural processes take over → re-establish themselves）。干扰项 B 描述的是传统公园 'someone decides where every shrub goes'，正好是讲话人要对比否定的对象；C 的'专家全程精细管理'与 'get out of the way' 相反；D 把'留一点野性空间'夸大成'把整个市中心变森林'，是典型的过度引申，迷惑性在于讲话人确实提过'我不是要把每个市中心变成丛林'。

questions.question: What does the speaker imply by contrasting the neglected rail yard with a carefully maintained park?
options: Well-kept green spaces normally support a much wider range of wildlife than abandoned ones.
The main reason people value parks is the chance to observe rare birds at close range.
Human intervention is often unnecessary and may even hold back nature's own recovery.
Abandoned industrial sites are always more attractive than purpose-built recreational areas.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'within about twenty years, more than a hundred and fifty species of bird had been recorded there... nobody planted any of it. We just stopped interfering, and the place healed itself.' 数字考点在这里要'绕'：题目选项不写'一百五十种'，而问这个对比说明了什么。推理链：无人打理的废弃地反而鸟类众多 → 因为没人干预 → 人类插手往往没必要甚至妨碍自然恢复。答案 C 的 'human intervention is often unnecessary and may even hold back nature's own recovery' 正是对该数字的言外之意概括。干扰项 A 说'精心维护的绿地野生动物更多'，与例子的结论方向完全相反，是最强的迷惑项；B 说'人们重视公园是为了近距离看珍稀鸟'，原文无此动机；D 说'废弃地总是比休闲区更好看'，把个别案例夸大成'always'的绝对结论，属于过度引申。

questions.question: According to the speaker, which TWO advantages of bringing more wildness into cities does he mention? (Choose TWO)
options: A noticeable drop in temperature across neighbourhoods during the hottest months of summer.
A significant reduction in traffic congestion on the roads surrounding the city centre.

title: The Language of Lies: What Our Words Reveal
speaker: Dr. Laura Bennett
description: 说谎时的语言特征及其可靠性的心理学研究
transcript:
Right, let's start with a little test. Imagine someone telling you a story, and you suspect they're not being entirely honest. What do you look at? I dunno — most people say the same thing: the eyes. If they look away, they're lying. Well, I've spent about fifteen years studying this, and I'm gonna be straight with you, that's basically wrong. It's a kinda lovely idea, and it's in every film you've ever seen, but the evidence just doesn't back it up.

I'm Laura Bennett, and I work on language and deception — that is, what our words give away when we're not being straight with someone. And the first thing I want to do today is clear away some of the myths, 'cause they're surprisingly stubborn.

So, the eye-contact thing. Loads of studies have looked at it. And the finding, again and again, is that liars don't necessarily look away more than anyone else. In fact, some of them stare at you harder, precisely because they know the stereotype and they're, like, trying far too hard to seem honest. I mean, you can see the problem, can't you? If you believe a false clue, you'll misread an honest person as a liar, and a nervous liar as... well, who knows. It goes wrong in both directions.

Now, if the body's not giving much away, what about the words? This is where it gets interesting. When researchers analyse what people actually say, they do find differences — just not the ones you'd expect. Here's one. People who are lying tend to use fewer words like "I" and "me". And I don't mean they're being modest. It's this unconscious thing where they sorta pull themselves out of the story. They'll say "that happened" or "there was an argument" instead of "I did it" or "we argued". It's like they're editing themselves out of their own account. We call it psychological distance, and it shows up more often than you'd think.

And here's a number for you. In one set of experiments, um, the people who were deceiving others used first-person words roughly thirty percent less often than the people telling the truth. Thirty percent — that's a big gap in a study like this. But here's what I want you to take from that figure: it isn't about how often you say "I" as a party trick. What it tells us is that lying feels different from the inside. It's, uh, effortful. You're managing a version of events, keeping track of what you said, and that mental work quietly changes your language.

There's another shift as well. Liars often use more negative words — words like "angry" or "awful" — even when the story itself isn't especially negative. And their accounts tend to be shorter and less detailed. You ask them what happened and you get the bare bones, whereas a truthful person will wander a bit, throw in odd little details, mention a smell or a colour that doesn't matter. Sounds counterintuitive, right? You'd think a liar would pile on the detail to convince you. But making stuff up is hard work, so they keep it simple. Makes sense when you put it that way.

So, can we use all this to catch a liar? Well, if you wanna judge one person from their word choice, honestly, no. And here's the bit people don't like. Every one of these cues is a tendency, not a rule. Plenty of honest people speak in short, low-detail sentences. Plenty of liars are calm and fluent. If you take a single individual and try to read them from their language, you'll be right barely more often than if you flipped a coin. That's not a failure of the research. It's just the reality of human behaviour.

But the research is still useful. Where it helps is with larger patterns — a whole set of statements, or comparing one account against another over time. If a story keeps changing shape, if the details keep shifting, that's worth noticing. And, look, there's a serious point here. A lot of people are far too happy to announce that someone's lying based on nothing but a hunch about how they spoke. I worry about that. You've gotta be careful — once you start treating a vague linguistic tip-off as proof, you can do real damage to someone who's telling the truth.

So what do I want you to take away? Be a little more humble about your own instincts. That feeling that something sounds off might be right, but it might just be a stereotype doing its work. Pay attention to consistency over time rather than a single moment. And if you're ever in a position where it really matters — a job interview, a dispute, anything serious — don't rely on folk wisdom about shifty eyes. Ask better questions, check the facts, and give people a fair hearing. Our words do reveal things, just not in the simple way the films would have you believe. Thank you.

title: Grid Locked: Why Fixing the Power Grid Is Harder Than It Sounds
speaker: Michael Torres
description: 电网升级的技术、经济与监管障碍
transcript:
Right, so here's a little thought experiment. You flip a switch, the light comes on, and you think nothing of it. Well, I want you to think about it again. Behind that tiny click is this enormous, mostly invisible machine — the power grid — and honestly, it's one of the most overlooked bits of engineering on the planet. I'm Michael Torres, and I've spent my whole career trying to keep that machine from falling over.

Now, when most people picture the grid, they picture, like, big power stations and pylons marching off into the distance. And that's not wrong, but it's the old picture. You see, the whole thing was built around one simple idea: a handful of big plants make electricity, and it flows one way, outward, to the rest of us. Kinda like a one-way street. That worked fine for decades. But then we started putting solar panels on roofs, and wind farms out in the middle of nowhere, and suddenly power wants to move in both directions. And the thing is, the grid was never built for that.

Let me put it another way. Picture a motorway designed for steady streams of cars all heading into town. Now imagine thousands of little vans and delivery trucks feeding in from every side, going every which way. What do you get? Jams. And that's basically what's happening on the grid. We've got generation in places the old wires never expected, so the lines get congested. You know, you can have a wind farm producing cheap power and still be unable to move it to the city that needs it. I mean, the energy's right there. It just can't get outta the wind farm and into the wires.

So the obvious answer seems to be: build more lines. And look, partly that's true. But here's where it gets painful. Putting up a transmission line is not, you know, like putting up a garden fence. First you've gotta get permission — and I don't mean one signature. I mean dozens of agencies, layers of rules, public hearings, and a whole lot of argument. There's a stack of paperwork taller than most people realise. In a lot of places, getting one new line approved can take the better part of a decade. A decade! That's long enough to, you know, raise a kid through primary school, just to get permission to start digging. And that number isn't there to scare you. What it tells you is that the bottleneck isn't really about engineering at all.

And then there's the money, which is just as messy. Who pays for all this? Sounds like a boring question, but it's actually the crux of the whole thing. See, power lines don't respect borders. A line might start in one state, cross a second, and benefit a third. So everybody wants the electricity, but, uh, nobody wanna pay for a line that mostly helps somebody else. And nobody wants a giant pylon at the end of their street, either. Basically, the costs stay local while the benefits get spread around, and that mismatch makes everybody dig their heels in.

Now here's the twist I find genuinely fascinating. You'd assume the hard part is the technology — that we're waiting for some brilliant invention to make the grid smart. But, well, we've already got most of the technology. The transformers, the sensors, the high-voltage cables — they exist. What we're short of is permission and coordination. It's paperwork and politics, not physics. Sort of ironic, really, when you think about it. I dunno about you, but I find that both frustrating and sorta hopeful, 'cause paperwork is something you can actually fix.

So where does that leave us? Look, I'm not gonna stand here and tell you it's easy. It isn't. But I think the first step is to stop seeing the grid as a pile of separate bits owned by separate people, and start seeing it as one shared system. Streamline the permitting, yes, but keep the safeguards that protect communities. Plan ahead instead of patching things together at the last minute. And accept that keeping the lights on is, you know, a collective job. Next time you flip that switch, spare a thought for the invisible machine behind it. It deserves a bit more of our attention. Thank you.

title: The Attention Economy: When Your Focus Is the Product
speaker: Priya Sharma
description: 注意力经济如何重塑媒体、广告与我们的心智
transcript:
Right, let me start with a question. How many of you, when you woke up this morning, reached for your phone before you'd even, you know, had a drink of water? Yeah. Most of you. Well, don't feel bad — I do it too. But I want to look at what that little habit actually means, because it's not just a habit. It's the engine of a whole industry. I'm Priya Sharma, and I study the way digital products compete for our attention.

Here's the idea I want you to sit with. When something online is free — a search engine, a social network, a news site — you tend to think, well, great, free stuff. But there's no such thing as free, really. If you're not paying with money, you're paying with something else. And that something is your attention. You know the old saying: if the product is free, you're the product? I'd go one step further. It's not just that you're the product. Your focus is the product. That's literally what's being bought and sold.

Let me unpack that. These companies make their money from advertising, right? And what an advertiser wants is for you to look at an ad — ideally for a while, and ideally when you're actually paying attention. So the platform's job is to get your eyes on the screen and keep them there. And the thing is, they've gotta do it better than their rivals, every single day. I mean, these are some of the smartest people around, working with enormous budgets, and their entire brief is: make it hard to look away.

Now, how do they do it? Well, there are a few tricks, and once you see them you can't unsee them. First, there's the endless feed — you know, you scroll and scroll and there's no bottom, no natural stopping point. Then there are notifications — like, little pings that pull you back in. And then the big one: variable rewards. Sometimes you open an app and there's something exciting waiting, sometimes there's nothing. That unpredictability is, uh, basically the same trick that makes slot machines so addictive. You keep checking 'cause you never know what you'll get. Sorta clever, sorta sinister, depending on how you look at it.

Here's a number I think is more revealing than it looks. Researchers reckon the average person checks their phone around fifty times a day. Now, fifty sounds like a lot, but honestly, that's not the bit I want you to focus on. What strikes me is that most of those checks aren't decisions at all. You don't think, right, I shall now check my phone. Your hand just does it. So the figure isn't really about how busy we are. It's about how much of our behaviour has quietly become automatic. We're not choosing to be interrupted; we've been trained to expect the interruption. Next time you reach for it, you might wanna notice whether you actually meant to.

And that has a cost, but not the cost you'd expect. It's not just that we waste time, though we do. The deeper cost is what happens to our minds. When you're used to constant, quick stimulation, sustained attention starts to feel, well, painful. Sitting with one difficult idea for twenty minutes feels unbearable. We've sort of forgotten how to be bored, and boredom, it turns out, is where a lot of good thinking happens. I dunno about you, but that worries me more than the lost hours.

Now here's the twist. The business model doesn't just waste our time — it shapes what we see. 'Cause the things that hold attention best are usually the things that make us feel something strong: outrage, fear, novelty, surprise. So the system quietly favours the extreme over the measured, the loud over the careful. And look, that's not a conspiracy. Nobody's sitting in a room going, let's make everybody angry. It's just that angry, startling stuff keeps people scrolling, so the machine promotes it over and over. Basically, what we give our attention to ends up shaping what we believe about the world and about each other.

So where does that leave us? I'm not gonna tell you to throw your phone in the bin — that's not realistic, and I'm not sure I'd do it myself. But I do think we should get deliberate. Turn off the notifications you don't need. Notice when your hand reaches for the phone without you. Give yourself a bit of real boredom now and then. Look, your attention is yours. It's probably the most valuable thing you own. Once you realise it's being traded, you can start deciding, for yourself, who gets to spend it. Thank you.

questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'the average person checks their phone around fifty times a day... What strikes me is that most of those checks aren't decisions at all. Your hand just does it... the figure isn't really about how busy we are. It's about how much of our behaviour has quietly become automatic.' 数字考点要'绕'：选项不写'五十次'说明了什么，而问这个数字的言外之意。推理链：一天五十次 → 讲话人强调关键不在数字大小，而在'大多数查看根本不是决定、手自己就动了' → 说明行为已自动化。答案 B 的 'much of our phone use has become automatic instead of deliberate choices' 正是对 'aren't decisions at all / quietly become automatic' 的同义替换。干扰项 A 说'人们比以前更忙'，讲话人明确否认 'isn't really about how busy we are'，是最贴合数字直觉的强迷惑项；C 说'该造续航更久的手机'，原文毫无提及，属于无中生有；D 说'只在有紧急消息时才查看'，与 'most checks aren't decisions' 直接矛盾，是把'查看'合理化为有目的行为的错误推断。

questions.question: What does the speaker suggest about the link between intense emotions and the content platforms promote?
options: Material provoking strong reactions gets amplified, quietly skewing what people come to believe.
The platforms secretly conspire in meetings to make all of their users feel angry.
Calm and carefully reasoned content is promoted because it keeps people scrolling the longest.
Anger is the only emotion that digital companies are technically able to measure.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'the things that hold attention best are usually the things that make us feel something strong: outrage, fear, novelty, surprise. So the system quietly favours the extreme over the measured... angry, startling stuff keeps people scrolling, so the machine promotes it over and over. Basically, what we give our attention to ends up shaping what we believe.' 推理链：强烈情绪最能留住注意力 → 系统反复推送极端内容 → 进而塑造我们的信念。答案 A 的 'material provoking strong reactions gets amplified, quietly skewing what people come to believe' 精准对应 'favours the extreme / promotes it over and over / shaping what we believe'。干扰项 B 说'平台开会密谋让用户生气'，讲话人明确否认 'that's not a conspiracy. Nobody's sitting in a room going, let's make everybody angry'，这是抓住'愤怒'一词的断章取义；C 说'冷静理性的内容被推得最多'，与 'favours the extreme over the measured' 方向完全相反；D 说'愤怒是唯一能测量的情绪'，原文从未谈测量能力，属于无中生有加绝对化。

questions.question: According to the speaker, which TWO effects of the attention economy on people does she describe? (Choose TWO)
options: A sharp fall in the number of people who own and regularly use digital devices.
A weakening of the capacity for sustained thought as quick stimulation becomes the norm.
A serious shortage of raw materials for manufacturing the latest smartphones.
An information environment that favours extreme, emotionally charged material over calm content.
questions.explanation: 本题要求归纳'注意力经济对人的影响'的两个正确结论。音频关键句一：'When you're used to constant, quick stimulation, sustained attention starts to feel, well, painful... We've sort of forgotten how to be bored'，对应 B 的 'a weakening of the capacity for sustained thought as quick stimulation becomes the norm'（持续专注力变弱，同义替换 sustained attention feels painful → weakening capacity for sustained thought）。关键句二：'the system quietly favours the extreme over the measured, the loud over the careful'，对应 D 的 'an information environment that favours extreme, emotionally charged material over calm content'（极端情绪内容更受青睐）。干扰项 A 说'拥有数字设备的人数骤降'，与常识和原文'人人起床摸手机'完全相反，属于方向性错误；C 说'制造手机缺乏原材料'，原文根本没讨论硬件生产，是凭科技话题硬编的无关项，迷惑性在于它像一条像样的产业新闻，却答非所问。
